{{Short description|Subfield of quantum cryptography}}

[[File:Authenticated qubit.svg|thumb|A safe, authenticated [[qubit]].]]
'''Quantum authentication''' is the sub-field of [[quantum cryptography]] that aims to apply [[quantum information theory]] for the purpose of [[authentication]] of quantum messages, users or devices.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Zawadzki |first=Piotr |date=2018-11-19 |title=Quantum identity authentication without entanglement |journal=Quantum Information Processing |language=en |volume=18 |issue=1 |article-number=7 |doi=10.1007/s11128-018-2124-2 |issn=1573-1332|doi-access=free }}</ref> Counterintuitively, it refers to a different problem from the authentication of the classical channel assumed in [[QKD]] protocols, which doesn't natively require quantum resources.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Shor |first1=Peter W. |last2=Preskill |first2=John |date=2000-07-10 |title=Simple Proof of Security of the BB84 Quantum Key Distribution Protocol |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.441 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=85 |issue=2 |pages=441–444 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.85.441 |pmid=10991303 |arxiv=quant-ph/0003004 |bibcode=2000PhRvL..85..441S }}</ref> 

A number of [[Authentication protocol|authentication protocols]] have been proposed since the advent of quantum cryptography, often inspired by [[Quantum key distribution|quantum key distribution]] counterparts.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Lim |first1=Na-Hee |last2=Choi |first2=Ji-Woong |last3=Kang |first3=Min-Sung |last4=Yang |first4=Hyung-Jin |last5=Han |first5=Sang-Wook |date=2023-09-13 |title=Quantum authentication method based on key-controlled maximally mixed quantum state encryption |journal=EPJ Quantum Technology |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |page=35 |doi=10.1140/epjqt/s40507-023-00193-y |bibcode=2023EPJQT..10...35L |issn=2196-0763|doi-access=free }}</ref> Ongoing research aims to both design new schemes and experimentally implement already proposed ones, as the technologies needed are mostly still under development.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Dutta |first1=Arindam |last2=Pathak |first2=Anirban |date=2022-11-07 |title=A short review on quantum identity authentication protocols: how would Bob know that he is talking with Alice? |journal=Quantum Information Processing |language=en |volume=21 |issue=11 |page=369 |doi=10.1007/s11128-022-03717-0 |arxiv=2112.04234 |bibcode=2022QuIP...21..369D |issn=1573-1332}}</ref> 

== History ==
The first quantum authentication protocol was proposed in 1995, based on [[oblivious transfer]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Crépeau |first1=Claude |last2=Salvail |first2=Louis |date=1995 |editor-last=Guillou |editor-first=Louis C. |chapter=Quantum Oblivious Mutual Identification |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=921 |editor2-last=Quisquater |editor2-first=Jean-Jacques |title=Advances in Cryptology — EUROCRYPT '95 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-49264-X_11 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=133–146 |doi=10.1007/3-540-49264-X_11 |isbn=978-3-540-49264-1}}</ref> Subsequent results in [[quantum cryptography]] showed that unconditionally secure two-party oblivious transfer in the quantum setting is impossible, limiting the feasibility of such constructions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lo |first=Hoi-Kwong |date=1997-08-01 |title=Insecurity of quantum secure computations |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.56.1154 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=56 |issue=2 |pages=1154–1162 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.56.1154 |arxiv=quant-ph/9611031 |bibcode=1997PhRvA..56.1154L }}</ref>

Early work also addressed the broader problem of quantum [[message authentication]]. It was proposed that [[Quantum state|quantum states]] can be authenticated against tampering using [[Symmetric-key algorithm|symmetric-key]] techniques, but that general quantum public-key authentication is not achievable without additional assumptions or restricted adversarial models.<ref name=":0">
{{cite book |author=H. Barnum, C. Crepau |chapter=Authentication of quantum messages |title=The 43rd Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, 2002. Proceedings.| year=2002 |pages=449–458 |doi=10.1109/sfcs.2002.1181969 |arxiv=quant-ph/0205128 |bibcode=2002sfcs.conf...46B |isbn=0-7695-1822-2 }}
</ref> These results also influenced following work on quantum digital signatures, using pre-distributed quantum states and restricted security assumptions.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last1=Okamoto |first1=Tatsuaki |last2=Tanaka |first2=Keisuke |last3=Uchiyama |first3=Shigenori |date=2000 |editor-last=Bellare |editor-first=Mihir |chapter=Quantum Public-Key Cryptosystems |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=1880 |title=Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO 2000 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/3-540-44598-6_9 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=147–165 |doi=10.1007/3-540-44598-6_9 |isbn=978-3-540-44598-2}}</ref>

Limited activity on quantum identity authentication (QIA) continued in the late 1990s, followed by a marked increase in proposals from the early 2000s onward.<ref name=":4" /> Many of these early QIA protocols were motivated by developments in [[quantum key distribution]] and typically assumed pre-shared [[Quantum entanglement|entanglement]] or conjugate coding techniques; research on quantum message authentication and [[Digital signature|digital signatures]] also continued, focusing on reducing costs and formalizing security.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clarke |first1=Patrick J. |last2=Collins |first2=Robert J. |last3=Dunjko |first3=Vedran |last4=Andersson |first4=Erika |last5=Jeffers |first5=John |last6=Buller |first6=Gerald S. |date=2012-11-06 |title=Experimental demonstration of quantum digital signatures using phase-encoded coherent states of light |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=3 |issue=1 |page=1174 |doi=10.1038/ncomms2172  |doi-access=free|pmid=23132024 |pmc=3493646 |arxiv=1306.0879 |bibcode=2012NatCo...3.1174C |issn=2041-1723}}</ref> More technologies were explored, such as entanglement swapping, multipartite entanglement and trusted third-party schemes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ljunggren |first1=Daniel |last2=Bourennane |first2=Mohamed |last3=Karlsson |first3=Anders |date=2000-07-13 |title=Authority-based user authentication in quantum key distribution |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.62.022305 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=62 |issue=2 |article-number=022305 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.62.022305 |bibcode=2000PhRvA..62b2305L |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Security analyses narrowed down the results by clarifying limitations related to [[Key (cryptography)|key]] reuse, composability and adversarial assumptions.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal |last1=Yehia |first1=Raja |last2=Diamanti |first2=Eleni |last3=Kerenidis |first3=Iordanis |date=2021-05-19 |title=Composable security for multipartite entanglement verification |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevA.103.052609 |journal=Physical Review A |volume=103 |issue=5 |article-number=052609 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.103.052609 |arxiv=2004.07679 |bibcode=2021PhRvA.103e2609Y }}</ref>

== Types of quantum authentication ==
Quantum authentication includes several related research areas that can be distinguished according to what is being authenticated: while some protocols authenticate the identity of a user or communicating party, others authenticate the integrity of transmitted [[quantum information]] or provide signature-like security. Although these areas share common [[Cryptography|cryptographic]] techniques, they address different security objectives and are often studied independently.<ref name=":10">{{Cite arXiv |last1=Battarbee |first1=Christopher |last2=Goswami |first2=Suchetana |last3=Kashefi |first3=Elham |last4=Doosti |first4=Mina |date=2026-06-29 |title=Authentication in Quantum Networks |class=quant-ph |eprint=2606.30636v1 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Quantum identity authentication ===
Quantum identity authentication (QIA) aims to authenticate a user, device or other communicating party by exploiting quantum-mechanical properties.<ref name=":3" /> Unlike classical [[Authentication protocol|authentication]], these protocols use quantum states during the authentication process, allowing eavesdropping or impersonation attempts to be detected through the disturbance introduced by [[quantum measurement|quantum measurements]].<ref name=":11">{{Cite journal |last1=Yuan |first1=Hao |last2=Liu |first2=Yi-min |last3=Pan |first3=Guo-zhu |last4=Zhang |first4=Gang |last5=Zhou |first5=Jun |last6=Zhang |first6=Zhan-jun |date=2014-11-01 |title=Quantum identity authentication based on ping-pong technique without entanglements |journal=Quantum Information Processing |language=en |volume=13 |issue=11 |pages=2535–2549 |doi=10.1007/s11128-014-0808-9 |bibcode=2014QuIP...13.2535Y |issn=1573-1332}}</ref>   

QIA protocols may provide one-way authentication, in which one party authenticates the other, or [[mutual authentication]], where both parties verify each other's identity. Many schemes are inspired by classical [[challenge-response authentication]], adapting them to quantum communication channels. They can also be classified as interactive or non-interactive depending on whether both parties must actively exchange information during the authentication phase.<ref name=":4" />

=== Quantum message authentication ===
In quantum message authentication (QMA), the aim is to authenticate the integrity and origin of quantum information sent over a [[quantum channel]]. Unlike classical message authentication, the message itself is a quantum state, which cannot generally be copied because of the [[no-cloning theorem]].<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |author=Wootters, W. K. and Zurek, W. H. |title=A single quantum cannot be cloned |journal=Nature |volume=299 |year=1982 |issue=5886 |pages=802–803 |doi=10.1038/299802a0|bibcode=1982Natur.299..802W |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/299802a0|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Quantum message authentication schemes therefore combine quantum encoding with a shared [[Key (cryptography)|secret key]], allowing the receiver to detect any modification or tampering of the transmitted state.<ref name=":1" /> If authentication fails, the receiver rejects the message rather than attempting to recover it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Ping |last2=Lu |first2=Yuxuan |last3=Lei |first3=Yikang |last4=Xiong |first4=Neal |date=2026 |title=Quantum Message Authentication Code Independent of Computational Difficulty |journal=IEEE Photonics Journal |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1109/JPHOT.2026.3654050 |bibcode=2026IPhoJ..18P4050W |issn=1943-0655|doi-access=free }}</ref> 

A foundational result by Barnum ''et al.'' showed that authentication of arbitrary quantum states necessarily implies their [[encryption]], meaning that a protocol capable of detecting tampering must also conceal the quantum information from an adversary; the same work also argued that unrestricted digital signatures for unknown quantum states are impossible without additional assumptions.<ref name=":0" />

=== Quantum digital signatures ===
{{Main|Quantum digital signature}}
Quantum digital signatures (QDS) are the quantum counterpart of classical [[Digital signature|digital signatures]]; they are intended to provide authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation while offering security based on quantum theory rather than computational assumptions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Xin |last2=Feng |first2=Dengguo |date=2005 |title=Quantum digital signature based on quantum one-way functions |journal=The 7th International Conference on Advanced Communication Technology, 2005, ICACT 2005. |volume=1 |pages=514–517 |doi=10.1109/ICACT.2005.245918 |bibcode=2005cact....1..159X }}</ref> Most QDS protocols authenticate classical messages using quantum states distributed during a setup phase, instead of attempting to sign arbitrary quantum states directly: this distinguishes them from QMA.<ref name=":0" />      

A QDS scheme consists of three probabilistic polynomial-time [[Quantum Turing machine|quantum Turing machines]] (<math>G</math>, <math>S</math>, <math>V</math>), where <math>G</math> is a key-generation algorithm that, on input <math>1^n</math>, outputs a pair (s, v) consisting of a secret signing key and a public verification key. <math>S</math> is a signing algorithm, <math>V</math> is a verification algorithm such that for all messages <math>m \in \{0,1\}^n</math> and all sufficiently large <math>n</math>,<blockquote><math>\Pr\left[V(m, S(m, s), v) = 1\right] \ge 1 - \frac{1}{\mathrm{poly}(n)}</math>,</blockquote>where the probability is taken over the internal [[randomness]] (classical and quantum) of (<math>G</math>, <math>S</math>, <math>V</math>).<ref name=":5" />

== Protocol classification ==
Quantum authentication protocols can be classified along multiple independent dimensions, including the quantum resources they employ or the underlying cryptographic primitive; these classification schemes are not mutually exclusive but highlight different aspects of protocol design, ranging from theoretical foundations to practical implementation constraints.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last1=Ghilen |first1=Aymen |last2=Belmabrouk |first2=Hafedh |last3=Bouallegue |first3=Ridha |chapter=Classification of quantum authentication protocols and calculation of their complexity |date=2014 |title=2014 15th International Conference on Sciences and Techniques of Automatic Control and Computer Engineering (STA) |pages=169–173 |doi=10.1109/STA.2014.7086669 |bibcode=2014sta..conf....9G |isbn=978-1-4799-5907-5 }}</ref>

=== By underlying cryptographic primitive === 
Quantum authentication protocols can be categorized according to the classical or quantum [[cryptographic primitive]] they are built on.<ref name=":6" /> Many schemes are derived from QKD, reusing [[conjugate coding]] or [[BB84]]-like states: in these constructions, authentication is often achieved as an additional layer on top of key establishment, or by embedding authentication information directly into quantum states exchanged during the protocol.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Jie |last2=Zhang |first2=Jie |last3=Qin |first3=Sujuan |last4=Jin |first4=Zhengping |date=2025 |title=A (t,n) threshold quantum secret sharing with authentication based on single photons |journal=Quantum Information Processing |language=en |volume=24 |issue=2 |page=61 |doi=10.1007/s11128-025-04672-2 |issn=1573-1332}}</ref>

[[File:Quantum Coin Flipping Protocol.png|thumb|536x536px|The [[quantum coin flipping]] protocol shares its structure with many quantum identity authentication protocols, since they consider Bob a valid user in case he can correctly select the basis on which to read the channel.]]

Other approaches are based on alternative primitives, including [[Quantum Secure Direct Communication|quantum secure direct communication]] (QSDC), [[quantum teleportation]]-based schemes, [[quantum secret sharing]], quantum private comparison, and quantum [[oblivious transfer]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dutta |first1=Arindam |last2=Pathak |first2=Anirban |date=2022-12-09 |title=Controlled secure direct quantum communication inspired scheme for quantum identity authentication |journal=Quantum Information Processing |language=en |volume=22 |issue=1 |page=13 |doi=10.1007/s11128-022-03767-4 |issn=1573-1332}}</ref> Each of these primitives introduces different structural assumptions and communication patterns. For instance, QSDC-based authentication protocols often aim to transmit authenticated messages directly through quantum states without first establishing a shared secret key, while secret-sharing-based constructions distribute authentication information across multiple parties to prevent unilateral forgery or impersonation.<ref name=":12">{{cite journal |author=Xu, F.  |title= Secure quantum key distribution with realistic devices|journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |volume=92 |year=2020 |issue= 2|article-number=025002|doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.92.025002 |arxiv=1903.09051 |bibcode= 2020RvMP...92b5002X}}</ref>

These different foundations lead to distinct trade-offs in terms of communication complexity, quantum channel usage, and trust assumptions: for example, protocols built on teleportation or [[Quantum entanglement|entanglement]] distribution may offer stronger theoretical guarantees or richer functionality, but typically require more demanding infrastructure, such as reliable entanglement distribution and synchronization between participants.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last1=Chawla |first1=Diksha |last2=Mehra |first2=Pawan Singh |date=2024 |title=QAKA: A novel quantum authentication and key agreement (QAKA) protocol using quantum entanglement for secure communication among IoT devices |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/ett.4957 |journal=Transactions on Emerging Telecommunications Technologies |language=en |volume=35 |issue=3 |article-number=e4957 |doi=10.1002/ett.4957 |issn=2161-3915}}</ref>

=== By quantum resources ===
[[File:EntanglementSwappingSketch.png|thumb|A simple sketch of entanglement swapping.]]
Another classification considers the physical quantum resources required for protocol execution.<ref name=":6" /> Early quantum authentication proposals frequently relied on pre-shared entanglement, especially [[Bell state|Bell pairs]], as a fundamental resource for establishing correlations that cannot be classically replicated: these entangled-pair-based schemes often assume that entanglement is distributed in advance between legitimate parties and later consumed during authentication.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shen |first1=Dongsu |last2=Ma |first2=Wenping |last3=Yin |first3=Xunru |last4=Li |first4=Xiaoping |date=2013-06-01 |title=Quantum Dialogue with Authentication Based on Bell States |journal=International Journal of Theoretical Physics |language=en |volume=52 |issue=6 |pages=1825–1835 |doi=10.1007/s10773-012-1276-6 |bibcode=2013IJTP...52.1825S |issn=1572-9575}}</ref>

Following research extended these ideas to [[multipartite entanglement]] structures, such as [[Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger state|Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) states]], which allow authentication schemes involving multiple participants or distributed verification processes.<ref name=":7" /> More sophisticated constructions also incorporate [[entanglement swapping]], enabling to dynamically entangle parties that have never directly interacted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Penghao |first1=Niu |last2=Yuan |first2=Chen |last3=Chong |first3=Li |date=2016-01-01 |title=Quantum Authentication Scheme Based on Entanglement Swapping |journal=International Journal of Theoretical Physics |language=en |volume=55 |issue=1 |pages=302–312 |doi=10.1007/s10773-015-2662-7 |bibcode=2016IJTP...55..302P |issn=1572-9575}}</ref>

In contrast, a large family of more practical protocols avoids entanglement, instead relying on [[Single-photon source|single-photon]] or weak coherent pulse implementations, which are significantly easier to realize experimentally using existing optical technologies. These schemes are often closer to QKD implementations and are more compatible with current fiber-optic infrastructure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hong |first1=Chang ho |last2=Heo |first2=Jino |last3=Jang |first3=Jin Gak |last4=Kwon |first4=Daesung |date=2017-08-17 |title=Quantum identity authentication with single photon |journal=Quantum Information Processing |language=en |volume=16 |issue=10 |page=236 |doi=10.1007/s11128-017-1681-0 |bibcode=2017QuIP...16..236H |issn=1573-1332}}</ref>

More recent developments include semi-quantum authentication models, in which only one party (typically the sender or trusted authority) requires full quantum capabilities, while other participants are restricted to classical operations such as reflection, measurement in a fixed basis, or classical communication. This approach reduces hardware requirements and broadens potential deployment scenarios.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wen |first1=Xiao-Jun |last2=Zhao |first2=Xing-Qiang |last3=Gong |first3=Li-Hua |last4=Zhou |first4=Nan-Run |date=2019-07-01 |title=A semi-quantum authentication protocol for message and identity |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1612-202X/ab232c |journal=Laser Physics Letters |volume=16 |issue=7 |page=075206 |doi=10.1088/1612-202X/ab232c |bibcode=2019LaPhL..16g5206W |issn=1612-2011|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Moreover, newer research directions explore a quantum counterpart of [[Physical unclonable function|physical unclonable functions]] (PUFs), where inherently noisy or complex quantum systems serve as device-specific fingerprints.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Buhrman |first1=Harry |last2=Cleve |first2=Richard |last3=Watrous |first3=John |last4=de Wolf |first4=Ronald |date=2001-09-26 |title=Quantum Fingerprinting |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.167902 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=87 |issue=16 |article-number=167902 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.87.167902 |pmid=11690244 |arxiv=quant-ph/0102001 |bibcode=2001PhRvL..87p7902B }}</ref> These quantum PUF-based approaches aim to provide lightweight authentication mechanisms rooted in physical uniqueness rather than cryptographic computation.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last=M. Doosti, N. Kumar, M. Delavar, E. Kashefi |year=2021 |title=Client-server Identification Protocols with Quantum PUF |journal=ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing |publication-date=2021-09-30 |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=1–40 |doi=10.1145/3484197|arxiv=2006.04522 }}</ref>

Finally, [[quantum position verification]] is being explored as a tool for identity authentication.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bluhm |first1=Andreas |last2=Christandl |first2=Matthias |last3=Speelman |first3=Florian |date=2022 |title=A single-qubit position verification protocol that is secure against multi-qubit attacks |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-022-01577-0 |journal=Nature Physics |language=en |volume=18 |issue=6 |pages=623–626 |doi=10.1038/s41567-022-01577-0 |arxiv=2104.06301 |bibcode=2022NatPh..18..623B |issn=1745-2481}}</ref>

== Security == 
The security of quantum authentication protocols derives from fundamental properties of [[quantum mechanics]] instead of computational assumptions.<ref name=":16" /> The no-cloning theorem prevents an attacker from creating copies of unknown quantum states, and any measurement disturbs the measured system: any eavesdropping or tampering attempts are detected. This prevents adversaries from perfectly replicating authentication tokens encoded in quantum information.<ref name=":2" />

Another key property is the disturbance caused by measurement: any attempt to extract information from a quantum system generally introduces detectable disturbances. This ensures that eavesdropping or tampering during transmission can be identified with non-zero probability.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last=C. Portmann, R. Renner |title=Security in quantum cryptography |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/RevModPhys.94.025008 |journal=Rev. Mod. Phys. |publication-date=2022-06-29 |volume=94 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.94.025008|issue=2|article-number=025008 |publisher=American Physical Society |arxiv=2102.00021 |bibcode=2022RvMP...94b5008P }}</ref> In addition, many protocols rely on the impossibility of perfectly [[Quantum state discrimination|distinguishing non-orthogonal quantum states]], which limits an adversary's ability to infer encoded information without introducing errors.<ref name=":14">{{Cite book |last=M. Nielsen, I. Chuang |title=Quantum Computation and Quantum Information |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2000|pages=56–57}}</ref>

=== Threats ===
[[File:Entanglement network with a trusted authority and an eavesdropper.svg|thumb|402x402px|An example of a threat: eavesdropper Eve (E) can listen on the quantum channel between Alice (A) and Bob (B) while they practice entanglement swapping each respectively sharing the pair 1,2 and 3,4 with a trusted authority (T) inside their network, and then swapping with a and b.]]
Quantum authentication protocols are designed to resist a number of attacks, including impersonation, [[message forgery]], [[Replay attack|replay attacks]] and [[Man-in-the-middle attack|man-in-the-middle attacks]]. Replay attacks involve re-transmitting previously valid quantum or classical authentication transcripts to gain  access, while man-in-the-middle attacks attempt to intercept and modify quantum transmissions while impersonating both legitimate parties to each other. Depending on the specific protocol, attackers may also attempt state replacement attacks, where transmitted quantum states are substituted with dishonestly prepared ones designed to not be detected.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=González-Guillén |first1=Carlos E. |last2=González Vasco |first2=María Isabel |last3=Johnson |first3=Floyd |last4=Pérez del Pozo |first4=Ángel L. |date=2021-03-25 |title=An Attack on Zawadzki's Quantum Authentication Scheme |journal=Entropy |language=en |volume=23 |issue=4 |page=389 |doi=10.3390/e23040389 |doi-access=free |pmid=33805925 |pmc=8064377 |bibcode=2021Entrp..23..389G |issn=1099-4300 }}</ref>   

Security analyses typically distinguish between external adversaries and dishonest insiders. In the second case, even legitimate participants could deviate from the protocol in an attempt to cheat, which significantly complicates security proofs. Formal guarantees therefore depend strongly on the chosen adversarial model and assumptions about participant behavior.<ref name=":9" />

=== Security assumptions ===
Despite relying on quantum-mechanical principles, most quantum authentication protocols require additional assumptions beyond the laws of physics alone. A common requirement is the existence of an authenticated classical channel, which ensures that classical messages exchanged during the protocol cannot be tampered with without being detected. This assumption is also standard in [[quantum key distribution]] and is typically enforced using classical authentication codes or pre-shared keys.<ref name=":8" />

Other assumptions include the availability of pre-shared secret keys or quantum states, trusted initialization phases, or the presence of a [[Trusted third party|trusted third party]] responsible for distributing or verifying authentication material. Some protocols also assume limited quantum capabilities for adversaries or restricted access to quantum memory, although such assumptions are generally considered stronger. These assumptions vary widely across protocols, and reducing them while maintaining strong security guarantees remains an active area of research, particularly in the context of composable security.<ref name=":9" />

== Experimental implementations ==
[[File:Quantum Entanglement Experiment via Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC).jpg|thumb|347x347px|Example setup for an experiment using entanglement, the same components can be used for entanglement-based quantum authentication.]]
Experimental realizations of quantum authentication protocols have so far been primarily implemented using [[optical fiber]] systems, which remain the most mature and practical platform for quantum communication. These implementations often adapt existing [[Quantum key distribution|QKD]] infrastructure, leveraging similar hardware such as photon sources, [[Beam splitter|beam splitters]], and single-photon detectors.<ref name=":11" /> Practical implementations have also been developed for quantum PUFs.<ref name=":13" />

In many cases, quantum authentication mechanisms have been integrated into existing QKD testbeds, allowing researchers to evaluate authentication performance alongside key distribution functionality.<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last=Termos |first=Hassan |date=2024-05-26 |title=Quantum Authentication Evolution: Novel Approaches for Securing Quantum Key Distribution |journal=Entropy |language=en |volume=26 |issue=6 |page=447 |doi=10.3390/e26060447 |doi-access=free |pmid=38920455 |pmc=11203336 |bibcode=2024Entrp..26..447T |issn=1099-4300 }}</ref> Ongoing experimental work focuses on extending transmission distances, improving noise tolerance, increasing key and state efficiency, and ensuring compatibility with emerging quantum network architectures, including early-stage quantum internet prototypes.<ref name=":12" />

== Applications ==
Quantum authentication has been proposed as a building block for secure quantum communication infrastructures. By providing authentication of users, devices or quantum messages, it complements confidentiality mechanisms such as quantum key distribution.<ref name=":15" /> 

In QKD [[Quantum network|networks]], authentication ensures that legitimate parties can securely establish keys without interference during initial communication. In a broader [[Quantum Internet|quantum internet]] context, authentication mechanisms are expected to play a central role in securing routing, entanglement distribution, and inter-network communication between heterogeneous quantum devices.<ref name=":10" />

Additional proposed applications include distributed quantum computing environments, where authentication is necessary to verify participating nodes and ensure integrity of distributed quantum operations. Similar considerations arise in [[internet of things]] systems incorporating quantum or optical devices, where lightweight authentication mechanisms may be required for large-scale deployment.<ref name=":7" />

== Challenges ==
Despite significant theoretical progress, quantum authentication protocols face several open technical and practical challenges. A major limitation is the lack of practical [[quantum memory]], which restricts protocols that require long-term storage of quantum states or delayed verification procedures. Most current implementations must therefore operate in real time or rely on immediate measurement, limiting design flexibility.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunjko |first1=Vedran |last2=Wallden |first2=Petros |last3=Andersson |first3=Erika |date=2014-01-31 |title=Quantum Digital Signatures without Quantum Memory |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.040502 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=112 |issue=4 |article-number=040502 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.112.040502 |pmid=24580426 |arxiv=1309.1375 |bibcode=2014PhRvL.112d0502D }}</ref>

[[Quantum noise]] and [[Quantum decoherence|decoherence]] in communication channels also remain as significant obstacles, particularly over long distances or in non-ideal environmental conditions. These effects can increase error rates and complicate the reliable detection of malicious interference versus natural noise.<ref name=":12" />

[[Scalability]] is another key challenge, as many protocols that work well in small-scale laboratory settings become difficult to extend to large networks with many users and devices. Issues such as synchronization, resource distribution, and network management become increasingly complex as system size grows.<ref name=":10" />

Finally, composable security for quantum authentication protocols is still an active research area. While many schemes are proven secure in isolated models, ensuring that they remain secure when composed with other cryptographic primitives (such as QKD or quantum signatures) remains non-trivial and is essential for building fully secure quantum networks.<ref name=":9" />
